q: What are vanishing and exploding gradients and how do you fix them?
a: Backprop multiplies per-layer factors, so gradients shrink (vanish) or grow (explode) exponentially with depth or sequence length. Vanishing: early layers stop learning. Exploding: NaN losses. Fixes: ReLU-family activations, He/Xavier initialisation, BatchNorm/LayerNorm, residual connections, LSTM/GRU for sequences, gradient clipping and lower learning rates for explosion.

q: Why can't you initialise all weights to zero?
a: All neurons in a layer would compute the same output and get the same gradient, so they stay identical forever: symmetry is never broken and the layer acts like one neuron. Weights need random initialisation (biases may be zero).

Both scale random weights to keep activation variance stable across layers. Xavier/Glorot: Var(w) = 2/(n_in + n_out), suited to tanh/sigmoid. He/Kaiming: Var(w) = 2/n_in, suited to ReLU, which zeroes about half its inputs and therefore needs twice the variance.

q: How do residual connections help training?
a: With \(y = x + F(x)\), the derivative is \(1 + F'(x)\), so gradients always have an identity path through the block and don't vanish through depth. Each block only needs to learn a correction. This made 100+ layer ResNets and deep Transformers trainable.
If the gradient norm exceeds a threshold c, rescale it: \(g \leftarrow c\,g/\|g\|\). It prevents single huge updates from exploding gradients. Standard in RNNs and LLM training (c ≈ 1.0).
